guide.title: A timeout is not a failure
guide.subtitle: Why resending an uncertain request costs you a second message
guide.excerpt: Sending is accepted asynchronously and there is no de-duplication key. Retrying a request you are unsure about sends a second message and bills for it.

p: A successful send response means the platform has taken responsibility for the message and handed it to a provider. It does not mean the message has arrived, or even that it has left. Delivery is a later, separate event that arrives as a receipt.
This matters at the moment your client gives up waiting. By the time a socket times out, the request may already have been accepted and the message already sent.

sections.h: There is no retry safety net
p: The platform does not offer an idempotency key and does not de-duplicate requests. Sending the same request twice sends two messages and bills for both. That is a deliberate position rather than an omission: a de-duplication window would have to guess how long a caller might retry, and guessing wrong is worse than being explicit.

sections.h: What to do when a request times out
list: If you received a message ID, query its status or wait for the callback. Do not resend.
If you did not, look the recipient up in the message log by time window and number before doing anything. Do not resend.
A client-side timeout does not roll back a message the platform has already submitted, and a duplicate is billed like any other.

sections.h: Designing around it on your side
p: The reliable pattern is to generate your own key before you call, store it with the outcome, and treat "no answer" as unknown rather than as failure. Reconcile from the message log or from `GET /open/v1/usage` instead of from your own optimistic counter.
sections.scope: Request handling described here is the SMS send path. Email and WhatsApp are accepted through the console today.
